title: All Four Sets on Loan
setting: a music library that lends orchestral parts

post.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
post.title: I finish my late great-aunt's machines at night. The loans program I finished for a music library says all 4 sets of a symphony are on loan. Three of them are on the shelf.

blocks.text: My great-aunt Winifrith Torvaine built coin machines and clockwork figures for sixty years, and wrote small programs for local firms in her last ten. She died in the spring and left me her workshop. Every unfinished machine there has a paper work order tied on with string. I program on night shifts, and I finish them at night.

This work order came from the county music library. It lends orchestral parts, the sheet music for each player, to amateur orchestras. The pile for a whole orchestra is called a set, and each set lives in its own box with a number painted on the lid. One piece of music, such as a symphony, is called a title. A title can have one set or several.

Winifrith's program keeps one record per title. A record is one entry in the program's files, like a card in a card index. Her title card holds the name, the number of sets, and which orchestras have a set out.

The work order asked for reservations, which run in steps. An orchestra asks for a title. If a set is in, the program puts one aside for them; that is called a hold. If none is in, they join the title's waiting list, in the order they asked. When a set comes back, the first orchestra on the list gets a hold and an email.
I added holds to her card. Each line below is one thing the card keeps or does. *free* is how many sets the counter may lend, and *o* is the orchestra asking:

Title       name, sets: 4
            out: railway
            heldFor: nobody
            waiting: nobody
free()      0 if heldFor, else sets - out
lend(o)     if free() > 0: add o to out
reserve(o)  if free() > 0: heldFor = o
            else: add o to waiting

A held title lends nothing else, so nobody can walk off with the held set. Beside the card Winifrith had written, in pencil: *Lend the paper, never the music.* The program went in three weeks ago. Every hold so far had been on a title with one set, and each one worked.

The *Tidewater Symphony* has 4 sets. Box 1 is out with the railway orchestra; boxes 2, 3 and 4 were on the shelf. On Tuesday at 10:15 Pancratia, who runs the counter, took a phone reservation from the hospital orchestra, to collect a set on Saturday.
The counter stays open late on Thursdays. Its screen keeps one line per request: the time, who asked, the free sets and the answer:

19:40  youth orchestra     free 0 of 4  all sets on loan
                           waiting list, no. 1
19:52  teachers' orchestra free 0 of 4  all sets on loan
                           waiting list, no. 2
Wojslaw, the youth orchestra's librarian, pointed past the counter at the shelf: three boxes, 2, 3 and 4, with the symphony's name on each lid.
The shelf said three. The card said none.

With heldFor set, free() returns 0, so the screen says all sets on loan. On the shelf: boxes 2, 3 and 4. Box 1 is with the railway orchestra.

blocks.text: Pancratia kept box 2 back for Saturday, lent boxes 3 and 4 by hand on paper slips, and emailed me the screen at 21:10. The program still has both orchestras on its waiting list. What should I change before the library opens tomorrow?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: What you and Winifrith drew has a name: a model, the choice of what kinds of record a program keeps and what each kind holds. Yours has one kind, the title. Try this. List what the library knows about the symphony: its name, its composer, who has box 1, Tuesday's hold, the waiting list. Beside each, write whether it is true of the music, the same for all four boxes, or true of one box. Then look at your card. Where did the hold go, and which box does it hold? And when a box comes back with nobody at the counter, what can your card tell you about it?

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: The name and the composer: the music. Who has box 1: one box, but my card only knows that the railway orchestra has *a* set. The hold went on the card, and it holds no box at all. Pancratia says boxes often come back after hours through the night return box, a chute in the library door, with only the number on the lid to say which.

comments.author: u/just_count_svatopluk
comments.text: You're overthinking a cupboard of sheet music. The boxes have numbers painted on; the program doesn't need them. Your bug is one line: a hold sets free to 0. Count a hold as one more set out, the way a loan is, and on Thursday free comes out 2 of 4, the boxes that weren't kept back. One kind of record, one count, nothing new to go wrong. Our choir's music cupboard ran on a count like that for years.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Pancratia likes it: one line, and Thursday's screen would have matched what the counter could lend.

comments.author: u/card_per_box_notburga
comments.text: Give each box its own card instead. Copy the symphony's name, composer and notes onto all four, and put the loan or the hold on the box's own card. The counter has a box in its hands at every loan and every return, so give the program the same thing to hold.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Pancratia would rather keep the title card and write a set number on each hold: the lowest-numbered set that has no hold yet. At the counter they already keep the lowest-numbered box on the shelf back for each hold.

reply.prompt: The library opens again in the morning, and the hospital orchestra comes for its set on Saturday. What should Odgerel change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Count each hold as one more set out on the title's card, so the screen shows the free sets again.
options.part2: I changed one line: each hold now counts as one more set out. On the workbench, Thursday came out right: at 19:40 the screen said 2 of 4 free, and the counter lent box 3 to the youth orchestra and box 4 to the teachers' orchestra, with box 2 kept back. It went in on Friday morning, and Pancratia typed in the two paper slips. On Saturday at 10:00 the hospital orchestra collected box 2, and at 10:20 the chamber orchestra, with nothing free, joined the waiting list. On Monday at 09:00 box 1 lay in the night return box, its second horn part missing. The program took one set off the count, but it could not say whose loan had ended: the railway, youth, teachers' and hospital orchestras all still showed a set out. Pancratia rang all four librarians, and each searched their own players' folders before rehearsal. The railway orchestra's librarian found the horn part on Wednesday. The chamber orchestra got its hold and its email on Monday, as it should.
options.senior: Counting holds fixes the number on the screen and nothing about what the number is made of. The card still records that an orchestra has a set, never which one, so the moment a box comes back without its borrower standing at the counter, the record can't tell whose loan ended, and anything wrong with that box belongs to nobody. A count is a question you should ask of records that already exist, one per box; kept as a number on its own, it is right only until you need to know which.

options.text: Make title and set separate records: loans and holds on a set, the waiting list on the title.
options.part2: I split the card in two. The title's record keeps what is true of the music: its name, composer, notes and waiting list. Each set got its own record, linked to the title, with its box number and its loan or hold. A hold goes on the lowest-numbered set on the shelf. On the workbench, Tuesday's hold went on set 2, and at 19:40 the screen said 2 of 4 free and named set 3, then set 4 at 19:52. It went in on Friday morning, and Pancratia entered the paper slips as loans of sets 3 and 4. On Saturday at 10:00 the hospital orchestra collected set 2, and at 10:20 the chamber orchestra joined the waiting list. On Monday at 09:00 set 1 lay in the night return box, its second horn part missing. Its record named the railway orchestra, and their librarian found the part in a player's folder on Wednesday. The program put set 1 on hold for the chamber orchestra and emailed their librarian. At 11:00 the library added a note to the symphony, *mark in pencil only*, on one record. At 17:30 the fire brigade orchestra joined the waiting list; no box was free on the shelf.
options.senior: Model the kind of thing and each copy of it as separate records, with each copy linked to its kind: one title, many sets. Then put every fact on the record it is true of. The music's name, notes and the queue of orchestras waiting for it go on the title; where a box is, who has it and what is missing from it go on the set. A hold takes one set out, free sets are counted from the set records, and a box in the night return box tells you its own borrower. Nothing is stored twice, so nothing can disagree.

options.text: Give each box its own record, with the title's name, composer and notes copied onto all four.
options.part2: I gave each box its own record and copied the symphony's name, composer and notes onto all four; the waiting list is filed under the symphony's name. On the workbench, Thursday came out right: Tuesday's hold went on set 2, and at 19:40 the screen said 2 of 4 free and named set 3, then set 4 at 19:52. It went in on Friday morning, and Pancratia entered the paper slips. On Saturday at 10:00 the hospital orchestra collected set 2, and at 10:20 the chamber orchestra joined the waiting list. On Monday at 09:00 box 1 came back through the night return box, its second horn part missing; its record named the railway orchestra, whose librarian found the part on Wednesday, and the chamber orchestra got the hold and the email. At 11:00 the library added a note to the symphony, *mark in pencil only*, and Pancratia typed it on 4 records, one per box. All four were done this time. But every change to a title with several sets is now one edit per box, and the library has many such titles.
options.senior: A record per copy puts loans and holds where they belong, so it works. The cost is that facts about the music now live once per box, and every edit to the music must be made on every copy. Miss one and the boxes disagree about the same symphony: one says pencil only, three don't. That is the update anomaly of keeping copies of one fact. And the waiting list, filed under the name, is already a title record in all but name. Make it one, and link the boxes to it.

options.text: Keep the title's card, and give each hold a set number: the lowest-numbered set with no hold yet.
options.verdict: Names a box it can't see
options.part2: I kept the title's card and gave each hold a set number: the lowest-numbered set with no hold on it. On the workbench, Thursday came out right: 2 of 4 free at 19:40, and boxes 3 and 4 lent. It went in on Friday morning, and Tuesday's hold became a hold on set 1. Set 1 was out with the railway orchestra; the card knows who has a set, not which. On Saturday at 10:00 the screen told the hospital orchestra to collect set 1. Box 1 wasn't on the shelf, so Pancratia handed over box 2, kept back since Thursday, and the card now said the hospital orchestra had set 1. On Monday at 09:00 box 1 lay in the night return box, its second horn part missing. The card found set 1 on loan to the hospital orchestra and closed their loan. Pancratia, going by the card, emailed their librarian about the horn part, while box 2 sat on their music stands. The railway orchestra, who had returned box 1, still showed a loan. Pancratia untangled both by hand on Tuesday, and the railway orchestra's librarian found the horn part on Wednesday.
options.senior: A number on the hold is a promise about a box the card can't see. Loans still live on the title, so the card doesn't know which boxes are out, and the lowest-numbered set may be the one an orchestra already has. From there the record and the shelf part ways, and every later step that trusts the number, a collection, a return, a letter about a missing part, lands on the wrong orchestra. Box numbers belong on records that know where each box is.

sim.title: Run the library's week on Winifrith's workbench
sim.lede: You're Odgerel at the workbench, replaying the library's week from Tuesday 10:00 through the design you pick. The symphony has 4 sets: box 1 is out with the railway orchestra, and boxes 2, 3 and 4 are on the shelf. Eight requests come, the ones the counter received from Tuesday to the following Monday, the same whatever the design: the hospital orchestra's reservation on Tuesday at 10:15; the youth and teachers' orchestras asking to borrow on Thursday at 19:40 and 19:52; the hospital orchestra collecting on Saturday at 10:00 and the chamber orchestra asking at 10:20; box 1 in the night return box on Monday at 09:00, its second horn part missing; a note added to the symphony at 11:00; the fire brigade orchestra asking at 17:30. As built, free() is 0 while heldFor is set, else 4 minus the sets out; an orchestra asking to borrow gets a set whenever free() is above 0, and the waiting list moves only when a set comes back. When the program names no box, the counter keeps the lowest-numbered box on the shelf back for each hold and lends the lowest-numbered box not kept back. A returned box the records can't match takes one set off the count and leaves every borrower in doubt. After Thursday, the as-built run shows what the card would have done had it stayed.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Step three times and read the title's record at 19:52: free 0 of 4, with boxes 3 and 4 on the shelf. Play the rest and read the waiting list. Then try counting holds and read whom box 1 came back from; numbering holds and read the loans the records get wrong; a record per box and read the records changed for Monday's note. Last, title and set records.

explain.oneLine: No set was on loan that the card said was. The hold went on the title, which stands for all four boxes at once, so free() fell to 0 and every set looked out. A hold, like a loan, belongs to one box; the waiting list belongs to the music.

steps.title: One card, two kinds of thing.
steps.text: The library deals in two kinds of thing. The music itself, the *Tidewater Symphony*, has a name, a composer and notes that are true of every copy. Each box is a thing too: it sits on one shelf or in one orchestra's rehearsal room, and has one borrower at a time. Winifrith's card kept only the first kind, and counted the second. With one set per title that is harmless, because the title and its only box are always in the same place. Every hold before Thursday had been on a one-set title, so nothing showed.

steps.title: A hold with no box holds every box.
steps.text: On Tuesday at 10:15 the reservation ran its steps. First, free() was 4 - 1 = 3, so a set was in. Second, the card set heldFor to the hospital orchestra; there was nowhere else to put it. Third, from then on free() returned 0, because a held title lends nothing else. At 19:40 and 19:52 on Thursday the youth and teachers' orchestras asked. free() said 0, the screen said all sets on loan, and both went on the waiting list, with box 2 kept back and boxes 3 and 4 free on the shelf. The rule was right for a title with one box and wrong for a title with four: a hold should take one box out, not the title.

steps.title: Which facts belong where.
steps.text: Sort every fact by what it is true of. The name, the composer, notes such as *mark in pencil only*, and the waiting list belong to the title: orchestras wait for the symphony, not for box 3. Where a box is, who has it, when it is due back and what is missing from it belong to the set. One title has many sets, and each set belongs to exactly one title. Programmers call this a one-to-many relationship. The IFLA library model draws the same line between a work and each item, a physical copy that may be many pieces, like a box of parts.

steps.title: Two records, linked.
steps.text: Make two kinds of record. The title's record holds the music's facts and its waiting list. Each set's record holds its box number, a link to its title, and its loan or hold. In code these are two classes (s5e04); in a database they are two tables, and the link is a foreign key, a column whose value must match a row in the other table. Then the steps change. Reserve: find the lowest-numbered set of this title on the shelf with no hold, and put the hold on that set; if there is none, add the orchestra to the title's waiting list. Lend: take a set with no loan and no hold, and put the loan on it. Return: close that set's own loan, then give the set a hold for the first orchestra waiting, and email them. What can go wrong: a set left with no title, or two holds on one set, so check both whenever a record is written.

steps.title: Counting and copying are the tempting half-fixes.
steps.text: Counting holds as sets out puts free() right, but the card still can't say which box anyone has, so a box from the night return box can't be matched to a loan. Giving each hold a set number, on a card that doesn't know which boxes are out, can name a box that is already out. Copying the title onto every box puts loans and holds in the right place, but writes the music's facts four times; miss one edit and the boxes disagree about the same symphony, the update anomaly from s3e10.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn at 19:52 on Thursday. One title record, the Tidewater Symphony, holds the name, the composer, the notes and the waiting list, which is empty. Four set records hang from it, each linked to the title: set 1 on loan to the railway orchestra, set 2 held for the hospital orchestra, set 3 on loan to the youth orchestra from 19:40, set 4 on loan to the teachers' orchestra from 19:52.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn at 19:52 on Thursday. The title's record holds what is true of the music and the waiting list, which is empty. Each set has its own record, linked to the title, holding its own loan or hold. The hold sits on set 2 alone, so sets 3 and 4 were free to lend at 19:40 and 19:52.

fix.title: The fix: a record for the title and a record for each set
fix.text: Split the card. The title's record keeps the name, the composer, the notes and the waiting list. Each set gets its own record with its box number, a link to its title, and at most one loan or one hold. Count free sets from the set records instead of keeping a number. Reserve puts a hold on one set on the shelf, or the orchestra on the title's waiting list; a return closes that set's own loan and offers the set to the first orchestra waiting. Enter Thursday's two paper slips as loans of sets 3 and 4, move Tuesday's hold onto set 2, and the record matches the shelf.

limits: The records are only as true as the check-in. A box that leaves without its loan recorded, or comes back through the night return box and is never checked in, makes the records drift from the shelf; the model can't see a box nobody records.
A waiting list on the title assumes any set will do. If sets come to differ in a way orchestras care about, such as their edition, a list for the title can hand an orchestra a set it can't use.

Two kinds of record means two to keep in step: a set must never point at a title that doesn't exist, and deleting a title must say what happens to its sets. A database's foreign key catches the first; the second needs a rule.

explain.seniorTake: Before you write a class, list the facts and ask what each one is true of. Things people borrow, fix, lose or return are usually copies; names, rules and queues for them are usually about the kind of thing. Model both, link each copy to its kind, and put each fact in exactly one place. A count is a question you ask the copies, not a number you keep beside them. A model that only has the kind works until the day a kind has more than one copy, and then the bug was there all along. A model that matches the world has nowhere for it to hide.

realWorld.title: IFLA LRM, 2017: the work
realWorld.text: The IFLA Library Reference Model defines a work as "The intellectual or artistic content of a distinct creation", and its scope note says "no single material object can be identified as the work". The *Tidewater Symphony* on the title's record is a work in that sense.

realWorld.title: IFLA LRM: the item
realWorld.text: The model defines an item as "An object or objects carrying signs intended to convey intellectual or artistic content", and its scope notes add that "an item may consist of multiple physical pieces or objects". A box of orchestral parts is one item made of many pieces.

realWorld.title: IFLA LRM: one form, many copies
realWorld.text: Between work and item the model keeps a manifestation: "A set of all carriers that are assumed to share the same characteristics as to intellectual or artistic content and aspects of physical form." Of the link down to items it says "each item is an exemplar of a single manifestation, while each manifestation is exemplified by one or more items": one-to-many.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL: the link between two tables
realWorld.text: PostgreSQL's documentation: "A foreign key constraint specifies that the values in a column (or a group of columns) must match the values appearing in some row of another table." And: "We say this maintains the referential integrity between two related tables." A set's link to its title, checked this way, can't point at a title that doesn't exist.

asked: How do you model a product and its physical copies?
When would you keep a count instead of one record per copy?
interview.answer: Start from the facts and ask what each is true of. A library has titles (the book or the symphony as a piece of work) and copies (the things on the shelf). Make them separate classes or tables: Title with name, author, notes and a waiting list; Copy with a barcode or box number, a link to its Title, and its state. Members borrow copies, so a Loan links a member to one copy with due dates; a Hold also sits on one copy. The waiting list is per title, because people wait for the book, not for copy 3. That is a one-to-many relationship, title to copies, enforced in a database by a foreign key. Availability is a query over the copies, not a stored number, so it can't drift. When a copy is returned, close that copy's loan and offer it to the first person waiting, with a conditional update so two holds can't land on one copy at once. If copies can differ in ways people care about, such as edition or format, add a level between title and copy, which the IFLA model calls a manifestation, and let a request say which it needs. Keep a plain count only for things that are truly interchangeable and never tracked one by one, such as identical consumables; anything lent and returned, inspected or lost needs its own record.

terms.def: An orchestra told none are free while a box sat on the shelf, not kept back for any hold.

terms.term: Loans the records get wrong (in the sim)
terms.def: Orchestras the records say have a set, or a given set, that they don't really have, or that really have a box the records don't show.
A box the counter leaves on the shelf for a hold. When the program names no box, the counter keeps back the lowest-numbered box on the shelf.

atWork: Look for a count stored beside something that has individual copies: stock 6, out 2 on a product that is lent and returned; seats 40, booked 38 on a room; licences 10, used 9 on a software product. Ask two questions. When one copy comes back damaged, can the records say who had it? When a copy is set aside for someone, which one is it? If the answer is no, or always the first one, the copies need their own records, linked to the product, and the count should be worked out from them. Read access to the class definitions or the database tables is enough to check. Search for fields named like count, available or out on a record that stands for a kind of thing, and for code that sets a whole product unavailable because of one booking. The same rule makes an asset inventory trustworthy for any audit: one record per asset, with its holder, so the total is a query nobody can edit by hand.

recall.prompt: A college's laptop loans desk keeps one record per laptop model: 12 in stock, 3 out, and the names of the three students who borrowed one. On Monday morning a laptop of that model turns up in the after-hours drop box with a cracked screen, and nobody can say whose it was. What is wrong with how the desk's data is shaped, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The record counts copies and names borrowers but never says which copy each borrower has, so a returned copy can't be matched to a loan
Give each physical laptop its own record (with its serial number), and put each loan on that copy's record
Keep the model's shared details once, on a model record each copy links to; work the counts out from the copies

recall.model: The record only counts copies and lists borrowers, so it can't tell which laptop each borrower has, and a laptop from the drop box can't be matched to a loan. Give each physical laptop its own record with its serial number, and put each loan on that copy's record, so the cracked laptop names its own borrower. Keep the model's shared details, its name, specs and any waiting list, once on a model record that each laptop record links to (a one-to-many link, a foreign key in a database), and work out the count from the copies instead of storing it.

recall.prompt: With the title and each set as separate records, which of these belongs on the title's record rather than on a set's?
options: The date a set is due back
The list of orchestras waiting for the symphony
recall.why: Orchestras wait for the music, not for box 3, so the waiting list is true of the title. A due date, a missing part and a hold are each true of one box, so they go on that set's record.

recall.prompt: A colleague wants one record per set, with the symphony's name, composer and notes copied into each, so the program has only one kind of record. It handled loans and holds correctly all week. What would you tell them before they ship it?

keyIdeas.idea: The music's facts are stored once per box, so every edit to the title must be made on every set's record
Miss one edit and the sets disagree about the same music: an update anomaly
Keep the title once in its own record and have each set link to it; the waiting list belongs there too

recall.model: It works for loans and holds, because those really are facts about one box. But the name, composer and notes are facts about the music, and now they are stored on every set's record, so every edit has to be made four times for this symphony. Miss one and the sets disagree about the same music: that is an update anomaly. Keep the title's facts once in a title record, give each set a link to it (a foreign key in a database), and put the waiting list on the title record too, since orchestras wait for the symphony, not for a box.

recall.prompt: As built, the hold on the title worked for three weeks before Thursday. Why?
options: Nobody had reserved anything until Tuesday
Every hold so far had been on a title with one set
The counter screen was switched off until Thursday
Holds only fail at the late Thursday counter
recall.why: With one set, the title and its only box are the same thing, so holding the title holds exactly one box. The symphony's four sets were the first time a hold on the title took more than one box out.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The split has held: every box has its own record linked to its title, and nothing has gone missing on paper since. In January the library bought 2 more sets of the Tidewater Symphony, a corrected printing with the wrong notes in the old horn parts fixed; they are sets 5 and 6, and their records link to the same title. In February the hospital orchestra joined the symphony's waiting list, wanting the corrected parts for a concert. On Tuesday old set 3 came back first, went on hold for them, and the program emailed their librarian. Their conductor sent it straight back.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the hospital orchestra get a set it couldn't use, and how should the records change?

keyIdeas.idea: The sets now differ in a way that matters, but the model has only the title and the set, so the waiting list treats any set as good enough
Add a level between title and set for each printing (IFLA's manifestation): the title has printings, each printing has sets
A request on the waiting list says which printing it needs, or any; a returned set goes to the first request it matches

coldCase.model: Until January all four sets were the same printing, so any set would do and a two-level model, title and set, was enough. Sets 5 and 6 differ from 1 to 4 in a way orchestras care about, but the model still treats any set of the title as good enough, so the first box back, old set 3, went to an orchestra that needed the corrected parts. Add a level between the title and its sets for each printing, what the IFLA model calls a manifestation: the title has two printings, and each printing has its own sets, linked to it. Then a request on the waiting list says which printing it needs, or any, and a returned set goes to the first request it matches. Set 3 would have gone to the next orchestra happy with the old parts, and the hospital orchestra would have waited for set 5 or 6.
